lesson.grammar_point: third conditional and past modals (should have, could have, must have)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: money or time set aside for what you cannot predict but know will happen
to raise a problem to somebody with more authority to decide about it
a gain you accept in exchange for a loss somewhere else, chosen on purpose
money already spent that cannot come back, and that should not decide anything now
the meeting after a project where a team works out what actually went wrong
the money a company needs to keep operating between paying its costs and being paid
how much a company stands to lose if one particular thing goes wrong
an early sign that something is going wrong, visible before the damage

paras: In January the firm had four projects running and a margin of eleven per cent on the fourth. In February a client offered a fifth. The partners looked at the numbers, saw a margin of eleven per cent again, and took it. Nobody in that meeting was careless and nobody hid anything. What nobody put on the table was the working capital, because the fifth project paid ninety days after the costs fell due, and the firm was already carrying two projects on the same terms.

The first red flag arrived in month two, and it did not look like one. A supplier asked for payment in advance. It was treated as a problem with that supplier rather than as information about the firm, which is the most expensive kind of mistake a project makes, because the information was already inside the building. By month three the contingency of four per cent had been spent, and the site manager escalated. The escalation stopped one level below the board, where somebody reasonable decided to wait for the quarter to close.

The board saw the file in month nine. By then the money was gone: eight months of it, and the eight months could not come back. What happened next is the part every post-mortem struggles with. The firm did not cut its losses, because the eight months felt like a reason to continue rather than what they actually were, which is a sunk cost. The project closed eleven months late at a margin of three point eight per cent. Every figure in this case was known inside the company before the end of the first quarter.

listenings.text: Before anybody speaks, let me tell you what I am not interested in this morning, which is who was to blame. Assume everybody in the case is competent and acting in good faith, because in my experience they usually are. The question I want is different. At what point had the decision already been taken, even though nobody in the room had said so yet? Now, a warning about a phrase I hear in every one of these discussions. They should have known. It is almost always the weakest sentence said in this room, because the information nearly always was there, in the building, on somebody's desk, in month two. So the real question is not whether they knew. It is why nobody acted on what they knew. By the end of the hour I want each of you to be able to name the exact moment when cutting their losses was still cheap, and to tell me what would have had to be true for somebody to do it.

The first red flag was a supplier who asked for payment in advance in month two, and I want to be honest about how we handled it: we treated it as a problem with that supplier. We did not read it as information about the project, and it was. That is the whole case, really. The part I still think about is month eight. By then the money was gone. It could not come back, it was not going to come back, and we kept making decisions as though it might, which cost us another four months on top of the eight. That is the definition of a sunk cost and I could have told you the definition at the time. Knowing the definition and behaving as if you know it are two different skills. What we do now is unglamorous. There is a post-mortem on every project, and the last question on the sheet is the one we used to leave blank: what we would do differently, written in full sentences, by the person who took the decision.
